datasets.title: Cell & Pathogen Data Sets
datasets.subtitle: All tabulated parameters are derived from first-principles electrostatics and corroborated by peer-reviewed biophysics literature. Membrane capacitance C<sub>m</sub> = ε<sub>r</sub>ε₀/d and the RC time constant τ = R·C<sub>m</sub>·(2σ<sub>e</sub>+σ<sub>i</sub>)/(2σ<sub>e</sub>·σ<sub>i</sub>) follow the corrected single-shell Schwan model; the double-shell nuclear extension gives a bandpass V<sub>m,nuc</sub> that peaks at f<sub>peak</sub> = 1/(2π√(τ<sub>out</sub>·τ<sub>ne</sub>)) rather than at DC. DEP crossover frequencies are computed from the single-shell Clausius-Mossotti factor K(ω); acoustic resonance frequencies use f<sub>res</sub> ≈ v<sub>wall</sub>/(2R) with viscoelastic Q-correction for bacteria. Medium conductivity σ<sub>e</sub> shifts τ and f<sub>c</sub> but leaves quasi-DC V<sub>m</sub> unchanged, a key invariance exploited for medium-independent lysis-field calibration. Joule heating, VSWR, and Maxwell-Garnett dense-suspension corrections are available in the Instrument panel.
datasets.subtitleNote: Computed at σ<sub>e</sub> = 1.5 S/m (physiological saline, 25 °C) · Kotnik & Miklavcic (2000, 2006) · Gascoyne & Vykoukal (2002) · Weaver & Chizmadzhev (1996) · Tsen et al. (2007) · Dykeman & Sankey (2008) · Pennes bioheat (1948)

cellLib.colErTitle: Effective membrane relative permittivity. Physical lipid bilayer ε_r ≈ 2-5; protein channels and pore contributions raise the effective value. Used in Cm = ε_r·ε₀/d.
cellLib.colSigITitle: Intracellular conductivity σ_i (S/m), sets RC asymmetry: τ = R·Cm·(2σ_e + σ_i)/(2σ_e·σ_i). Higher σ_i → shorter τ, higher f_c. Literature ranges: mammalian 0.3-0.7, bacteria 0.25-0.5, virions ~0.5 S/m
cellLib.colCmTitle: Membrane capacitance per area: Cm = ε_r·ε₀/d (F/m², shown as mF/m²). Drives the RC time constant τ. Physical lipid bilayer gives ~0.5-1 µF/cm²; effective Cm elevated by pore complexes and ion channels
cellLib.colFcTitle: Characteristic (−3 dB) frequency: f_c = 1/(2πτ). Above f_c the transmembrane voltage Vm rolls off as 1/f. Computed at σ_e = 1.5 S/m (saline); use the DataSets Media table for τ shifts in other media
cellLib.colFcrossTitle: First DEP crossover frequency, where Re[K(ω)] = 0 and dielectrophoretic force polarity reverses (pDEP to nDEP). Computed via single-shell Clausius-Mossotti model at σ_e = 1.5 S/m, ε_r = 80 (saline). ', ' indicates no crossing found in 1 kHz-10 GHz range.
cellLib.colFcross2Title: Second DEP crossover frequency, where Re[K(ω)] = 0 again above f_cross1. Occurs at high frequencies when membrane and cytoplasm permittivities dominate over conductivity (dielectric relaxation re-inverts K polarity). Relevant for GHz-band DEP separation. Ref: Pethig, Biomicrofluidics 4:022811 (2010). ', ' indicates no second crossing found.
cellLib.colVmThrTitle: Lysis threshold voltage V_m,thr, minimum sustained transmembrane potential for irreversible electroporation. Sets lysis field: E_lysis = V_m,thr / (1.5 × R). Cancer cells have lower thresholds due to structural membrane abnormalities
cellLib.colRnucTitle: Nuclear radius: double-shell model (mammalian nucleated cells only; RBC and bacteria/virus have no nucleus)
cellLib.colRhoTitle: Cell or virion density ρ (kg/m³), used in SAR: SAR = σ_i·α²·E²·dc/ρ, where α = 3σ_e/(2σ_e + σ_i) is the internal-field factor
cellLib.colQTitle: Mechanical quality factor, sharpness of resonance peak
cellLib.colEthrTitle: Theoretical RF field amplitude for capsid/cell-wall disruption at resonance. Tsen et al. experiments used femtosecond laser excitation, not RF; these V/cm values are extrapolations with no direct experimental basis.
cellLib.fNote4: f_res / Q / E_thr: acoustic resonance (bacteria/virus) · Tsen et al. (2007); Dykeman & Sankey (2008)

media.sectionTag: Extracellular conductivity σ<sub>e</sub> shifts τ and V<sub>m</sub>
media.colEpsRTip: Relative permittivity at ~1 MHz (Gabriel et al. 1996). Enters the DEP Clausius-Mossotti factor K(ω) as the medium dielectric baseline. Lower ε_r (e.g., blood: 64) shifts the DEP crossover frequency relative to saline. Not used in the Schwan Vm model, only in DEP force calculations.
media.colAlphaTip: Conductivity temperature coefficient: σ_e(T) = σ_e0 · (1 + α · (T − 37)). At the IAHT hyperthermia limit of 42°C this is a 7.5–14% rise in σ_e depending on medium, shifting τ and f_c proportionally. Critical for in-vivo protocols where tissue heats during pulse delivery. Culture media values approximate at ~2%/°C (NaCl-dominated ionic strength).
media.colEffect: Effect on τ / f<sub>c</sub> (quasi-DC V<sub>m</sub> unchanged), epithelial ref σ<sub>i</sub> ≈ 0.5 S/m
media.salineEffect: Reference baseline · τ and f<sub>c</sub> reference (V<sub>m,DC</sub> independent of medium)
media.salineUse: Standard in vitro assay medium · physiological approximation
media.bloodEffect: τ +16% · f<sub>c</sub> −14% (epithelial σ<sub>i</sub>≈0.5; bacteria ~10% (σ<sub>i</sub>≈0.3); virions ~0%, low-σ<sub>i</sub> cells barely affected) · V<sub>m,DC</sub> unchanged
media.bloodUse: Haematological applications · in vivo tumour vasculature
media.tissueEffect: τ +39% · f<sub>c</sub> −28% (epithelial σ<sub>i</sub>≈0.5; bacteria ~25% (σ<sub>i</sub>≈0.3); virions ~0.5%) · V<sub>m,DC</sub> unchanged · increased τ shifts fc lower
media.tissueUse: Solid tumour bulk / poorly-perfused tissue (note: DMEM ≈ 1.4-1.6 S/m, not used here)
media.waterEffect: τ ~200× longer · f<sub>c</sub> to ~5 kHz (epithelial σ<sub>i</sub>≈0.5 S/m); bacteria ~137× (σ<sub>i</sub>≈0.3); virions ~3-5× (σ<sub>i</sub>≪σ<sub>e</sub> → medium effect collapses)
media.dmemEffect: τ +1% · f<sub>c</sub> −1% (epithelial), effectively identical to saline · V<sub>m,DC</sub> unchanged
media.dmemUse: Standard adherent mammalian cell culture (HeLa, A549, MCF-7, HEK293)
media.pbsEffect: τ +3% · f<sub>c</sub> −3% (epithelial σ<sub>i</sub>≈0.5), near-identical to saline · V<sub>m,DC</sub> unchanged
media.pbsUse: Wash buffer, short-term electroporation assays, flow cytometry prep; no nutrients, not for extended culture
media.rpmiEffect: τ +2% · f<sub>c</sub> −2% (epithelial), negligible difference vs saline · V<sub>m,DC</sub> unchanged
media.rpmiUse: Suspension and haematological cell lines (HL-60, Jurkat, PBMC, LNCaP)
media.mhbEffect: τ +13% · f<sub>c</sub> −11% (epithelial σ<sub>i</sub>≈0.5); bacteria ~8% (σ<sub>i</sub>≈0.3); virions ~0.5% · V<sub>m,DC</sub> unchanged
media.mhbUse: CLSI/EUCAST bacterial susceptibility testing standard (E. coli, MRSA, Klebsiella)
media.fNote2: Only τ and f_c shift with medium; quasi-DC Vm is set by E and R only
media.fEq3: Large when σ_i ≈ σ_e · negligible when σ_i ≪ σ_e
media.fNote3: Epithelial cells (σ_i ≈ 0.5 S/m): large shift · Virions (σ_i ≪ σ_e): negligible shift

window.labelVmSel: Max V<sub>m</sub> selectivity at quasi-DC (<100 kHz), driven by size ratio R<sub>T</sub>/R<sub>H</sub>
window.labelTI: Therapeutic Index TI at quasi-DC, normalised by lysis thresholds (1.1 V / 0.70 V)
window.labelFreqDown: Selectivity decreases above f<sub>c</sub>(T), target rolls off before healthy cell
window.windowNote: Cancer lysis at ~311 V/cm · Healthy threshold at ~733 V/cm
window.fNote3: = (DR_T / DR_H) at fixed E · adeno vs hepatocyte: TI = (1.1 × 15)/(0.70 × 10) = 2.36× at quasi-DC

nucShell.sectionTag: Mammalian nucleated cells only · Kotnik & Miklavcic (2006)
nucShell.colRnucTitle: Nuclear radius: typically 40-60% of cell radius for mammalian cells
nucShell.colDneTitle: Nuclear envelope thickness (inner + outer membrane + lumen ≈ 40 nm total; d here is electrical effective thickness)
nucShell.colEpsNeTitle: Relative permittivity of nuclear envelope, elevated vs lipid bilayer due to nuclear pore complex contribution
nucShell.colSigNpTitle: Nucleoplasm conductivity: typically higher than cytoplasm due to dissolved chromatin and RNA
nucShell.colVthrNucTitle: Nuclear membrane disruption threshold voltage, cancer nuclei have thinner/leakier NE, lower threshold
nucShell.colFpeakTitle: Peak frequency of nuclear Vm bandpass: f_peak = 1 / (2π × √(τ_out × τ_ne)), nuclear Vm is maximised here, not at DC
nucShell.fEq4: Bandpass - zero at DC and at GHz, peaks at f_peak
nucShell.fNote4: Cancer nuclei: elevated N/C ratio → larger R_nuc → lower f_peak · σ_ne → 0 assumed (capacitive-limit model: NE treated as pure capacitor)

acousticRes.virusQNote: (enveloped lipid bilayer — fluid, no defined resonance; speculative model est. Non-enveloped icosahedral capsids: Q ≈ 25-30 in vacuo, Dykeman & Sankey 2010)
acousticRes.selRatioLabel: Theoretical selectivity at f<sub>res</sub>, healthy Schwan Vm → 0 at GHz
acousticRes.selLorentzianLabel:
Disruption = (E / Ethr) × L(f, fres, Q)
L peaks at 1.0 at fres
acousticRes.selRef: Ref: Tsen et al. (2007, 2012) · Dykeman & Sankey (2008)
acousticRes.fNote3: Schwan V_m → 0 via ωτ >> 1 at GHz, dispersive roll-off, not resonance

fieldGeo.geoParagraph: The Schwan model assumes a uniform, quasi-static electric field applied to a suspension of non-interacting spherical cells at low volume fraction. In clinical TTField devices (Optune®), 4 electrode arrays generate a rotating field at 100-300 kHz with amplitudes of 1-3 V/cm at depth; the field map is non-uniform and computed via FEM models of head conductivity. The ResoPulse simulator applies the uniform-field Schwan equation and is appropriate for well-mixed in vitro geometries (parallel-plate or four-electrode chambers).
fieldGeo.assumption1: Single-shell (Schwan) or double-shell (nuclear envelope) cell model
fieldGeo.assumption2: Uniform applied field (E constant in space)
fieldGeo.assumption4: Linear membrane response, below pore-formation threshold
fieldGeo.assumption5: Isotropic, homogeneous cytoplasm and extracellular medium
fieldGeo.assumption6: Temperature-corrected medium conductivity σ<sub>e</sub>(T) = σ<sub>e0</sub>·(1 + α·(T−37°C)); α = 2%/°C (saline), 1.7% (blood), 1.5% (tissue), 2.8% (water)
fieldGeo.assumption7: Blood perfusion cooling: λ<sub>perf</sub> = ω<sub>b</sub> × 63.9 / c<sub>p</sub> added to Newton cooling λ = 0.02 s⁻¹ in Pennes bioheat (Advanced panel: ω<sub>b</sub> = 0 for in vitro)
fieldGeo.assumption8: Dense suspension: Maxwell-Garnett correction σ<sub>e,eff</sub> = σ<sub>e</sub>·(1−φ)/(1+φ/2); φ = 0 (isolated cell) to 0.64 (random close-packing). Set via Cell Packing slider (Advanced panel)

thresholds.sectionTag: Constants used by the ResoPulse simulation engine
thresholds.drNourishingDesc: Sub-threshold biomodulation: PIEZO1 / Ca²⁺ activation (healthy cells only). SI score peaks at ~22.5% DR, falls to zero at 45%
thresholds.drApproachingDesc: Membrane stress onset, ion channel perturbation; pore-free but biologically active. Viable membrane
thresholds.drRevEpStateTitle: Reversible electroporation: transient aqueous pores form and reseal within ms-s. Sub-lethal; exploited for drug/gene delivery in clinical EP protocols (e.g., electrochemotherapy)
thresholds.drRevEpDesc: Reversible electroporation: pores open & reseal; drug/gene delivery window
thresholds.drVibratingDesc: Lysis countdown armed (target cell only); irreversible pore accumulation begins
thresholds.drLysingDesc: Disruption threshold crossed; lysis fires after protocol time N × t<sub>p</sub>/dc
thresholds.drSigmoidNote: Lysis probability sigmoid: P = 1 / (1 + exp(−(DR − 1.0) / 0.05)). At DR = 100% (Vm = V<sub>thr</sub>): P = 50%. At DR = 115%: P greater than 95%. The slope 0.05 reflects population spread in pore-formation kinetics across individual cells (Weaver & Chizmadzhev 1996).
thresholds.tiAblativeMode: Healthy cells also in lysis zone
thresholds.classColModeTitle: Default chart mode and parameter ranges auto-applied when this cell category is selected as the Experiment target. Schwan = RC charging model; IRE = irreversible EP; Resonance = Lorentzian acoustic model (bacteria/virus)
thresholds.classNote: Classification drives automatic slider ranges, waveform defaults, and chart mode when a preset is loaded in the Experiment Lab (see experimentDefaults.ts).
thresholds.uncVirusEffect: τ spans ~2×; treat f_c and TI as order-of-magnitude estimates
thresholds.uncBactEffect: τ spans ~1.7×; f_c reliable to ±30% in standard culture conditions
thresholds.uncMammalEffect: f_c reliable to ±15%; TI error ~0.3× at nominal TI = 2.36×
thresholds.uncNote: Dominant source: intracellular conductivity σ_i varies with cell cycle phase, culture conditions, and measurement method. Uncertainty bands are propagated into TI error bars shown in the SelectivityPanel.
thresholds.bmsSiBasis: PIEZO1 / Ca²⁺ sub-threshold activation, MAPK/ERK signalling
thresholds.bmsMteBasis: Acoustic pressure coupling, TRPV1 / cytoskeletal remodelling
thresholds.bmsMaBasis: T_ss 37 to 41°C nourishing window, HSP70 sub-threshold expression
thresholds.bmsNote: BMS is only meaningful at DR less than 45% (Nourishing / Approaching states). At DR 50% or above, electroporation dominates and BMS is superseded. Score 0.55 or above activates the nourishing glow on healthy cells in the simulation.

cta.note: Apply these parameters interactively in the simulation

tip.legendReference: Healthy mammalian reference cells. These are not 'bystander' cells, they are the limiting constraint on every protocol. The lysis field E_lysis,H sets the upper bound of the therapeutic window; any field above this value causes collateral damage regardless of target selectivity.
tip.legendCancer: Transformed mammalian cells. Membrane disordering (increased ε_r, reduced d) and elevated N/C ratio lower both V_m,thr and f_c. At quasi-DC the size ratio R_T/R_H drives Vm selectivity; the V_thr asymmetry compounds this into the Therapeutic Index. Both quantities degrade rapidly above f_c(T).
tip.legendBacteria: Prokaryotes: gram-negative (E. coli) and gram-positive (MRSA). The Schwan single-shell model is an approximation here: the peptidoglycan wall is a mechanically stiff viscoelastic shell that is not represented as a dielectric layer. Q ≈ 3-4 (viscoelastic damping), not 10-15 as for protein capsid virions.
tip.legendVirus: Enveloped / naked virions. R ≈ 60 nm means quasi-DC Vm = 1.5·E·R is very small, the Schwan model is valid but the driving amplitudes needed for lysis are impractically large. Acoustic resonance at ~10-12 GHz is currently inaccessible by RF hardware; those values are extrapolated from femtosecond-laser experiments (Tsen et al.).
tip.colCm: Cm = ε_r·ε₀/d. The physical lipid bilayer gives ~0.5-1 µF/cm²; effective Cm is elevated in cancer cells by nuclear pore complexes, ion channels and membrane disordering. A higher Cm lengthens τ and shifts f_c to lower frequencies, which contracts the usable frequency window.
tip.colFc: f_c = 1/(2πτ), the −3 dB roll-off frequency. Above f_c, Vm ∝ 1/f. For selective protocols the operating frequency should be below f_c(T) and ideally well below f_c(H) to maximise the TI. Computed at σ_e = 1.5 S/m; see the Media table for τ shifts in other buffers.
tip.colFcross: First DEP crossover: frequency where Re[K(ω)] = 0 and the dielectrophoretic force reverses direction (pDEP to nDEP). Below f_cross1: typically nDEP (cell repelled from field maxima). Above f_cross1: pDEP (cell attracted). Used in lab-on-chip cell sorting to separate live vs dead, or cancer vs normal.
tip.colFcross2: Second DEP crossover: frequency where Re[K(ω)] = 0 again above f_cross1. Occurs when high-frequency dielectric relaxation causes the membrane and cytoplasm permittivities to dominate over conductivity, re-inverting the K polarity back to nDEP. Relevant for GHz-band DEP microfluidic separation. Ref: Pethig (2010). ', ' indicates no second crossing found in the range.
tip.colVmThr: Minimum sustained transmembrane voltage for irreversible electroporation. Sets lysis field via E_lysis = V_m,thr / (1.5·R·cosθ). Cancer cells have lower thresholds due to membrane structural abnormalities, this V_thr asymmetry is the second source of Therapeutic Index gain beyond pure size ratio.
tip.colRnuc: Nuclear radius (mammalian nucleated cells only). The nuclear/cytoplasmic (N/C) volume ratio is elevated in cancer, this is an established histopathological marker (nuclear atypia). Higher N/C ratio → larger R_nuc → lower f_peak → nuclear Vm peak accessible at lower frequencies.
tip.colEr: Effective ε_r for the membrane shell. Physical lipid bilayer ε_r ≈ 2-5; elevated effective values (5-20) reflect contributions from nuclear pore complexes, glycoprotein channels, and membrane roughness. Only ε_r affects Cm; it does not appear in the Schwan Vm formula directly, only through τ.
tip.colSigI: Cytoplasmic conductivity: sets the RC asymmetry ratio (2σ_e+σ_i)/(2σ_e·σ_i). Higher σ_i relative to σ_e shortens τ and raises f_c. For bacteria σ_i ≈ 0.3-0.5 S/m; for mammalian cells 0.3-0.7 S/m. Uncertainty in σ_i is a primary source of model uncertainty for individual cells.
tip.colRho: Cell density: used in the SAR heating model: SAR = σ_i·α²·E²·dc/ρ where α = 3σ_e/(2σ_e+σ_i). Denser cells (bacteria, virions) have higher volumetric thermal inertia. For in-vitro assays the dominant thermal mass is the medium, not individual cells.
tip.colFres: Acoustic resonance frequency f_res ≈ v_wall/(2R), where v_wall is the effective elastic wave speed through the cell wall/capsid (~1000-1500 m/s). Values are literature-derived from femtosecond-laser Raman spectroscopy experiments (Tsen et al. 2007), not from RF hardware measurements.
tip.colQ: Mechanical quality factor Q = f_res / FWHM. Sets the sharpness of the resonance peak and the frequency tolerance required: at Q = 4, the −3 dB bandwidth is f_res/4. Bacteria Q ≈ 3-4 (viscoelastic peptidoglycan); viral capsids Q ≈ 25-30 (rigid icosahedral protein shell).
tip.colEthr: Theoretical field amplitude for capsid disruption at resonance. These values are extrapolated from femtosecond-laser irradiance experiments, the energy coupling mechanism for RF continuous-wave fields is fundamentally different (near-field ohmic vs photon absorption). Treat as an order-of-magnitude reference only.
tip.nucColRnuc: Nuclear radius. Together with R (cell radius), determines the N/C volume ratio φ_nuc = (R_nuc/R)³. Cancer cells typically have φ_nuc > 0.5, elevated N/C ratio is a defining histopathological feature of neoplasia (nuclear atypia) and directly raises the double-shell f_peak into a more accessible frequency range.
tip.nucColDne: Electrical effective thickness of the nuclear envelope, the actual double-membrane + perinuclear lumen spans ~40 nm, but the equivalent dielectric slab for capacitance purposes is thinner due to the high conductance of nuclear pore complexes. A thinner d_ne raises C_m,ne and lowers τ_ne.
tip.nucColEpsNe: Nuclear envelope effective permittivity. Elevated versus pure lipid bilayer (ε_r ≈ 2-5) because nuclear pore complexes (NPCs), ~120 MDa protein assemblies, contribute substantial polarisability. NPC density is ~10-40 per µm² in mammalian cells.
tip.nucColSigNp: Nucleoplasm conductivity: typically higher than cytoplasm due to dissolved chromatin, RNA, and ribosome contributions. Higher σ_np shortens τ_ne and raises f_peak, moving the nuclear Vm bandpass peak to higher frequencies where hardware can reach it.
tip.nucColVthrNuc: Nuclear membrane disruption voltage. Cancer nuclei have thinner, NPC-denser, structurally weakened envelopes, both V_thr,nuc and d_ne are reduced. Nuclear disruption at sub-cellular scale can trigger apoptotic cascades even when the outer membrane is intact (nuclear IRE concept).
tip.nucColFpeak: f_peak = 1/(2π√(τ_out · τ_ne)). This is NOT a resonance, it is the geometric mean of the two RC time constants, giving the frequency where the nuclear Vm bandpass peaks. Operating near f_peak maximises nuclear membrane stress relative to outer membrane stress. Note: f_peak is generally lower in cancer cells due to larger R_nuc.
tip.drStable: Ion channels are unperturbed; membrane polarisation is below the threshold for stretch-activated mechanosensors. Safe range for imaging, biomodulation scoring, and sub-lytic protocols. Vm/V_thr < 20%; no detectable change in membrane permeability via fluorescent dye exclusion assays.
tip.drNourishing: Sub-lytic biomodulation window, clinically relevant for tissue regeneration and electrostimulation protocols. PIEZO1 activation enhances endothelial nitric oxide production; Ca²⁺ influx drives MAPK/ERK signalling. SI score peaks at ~22.5% DR and decays to zero at 45%. No pore formation verified by calcein-AM exclusion.
tip.drApproaching: Lipid bilayer fluidity measurably increases (verified by fluorescence anisotropy). Peripheral membrane proteins begin conformational change. No electroporation pores form, this is a purely capacitive, reversible membrane stress state. Exists only transiently; membrane recovers within ~seconds of field removal.
tip.drRevEp: Transient aqueous pore formation, pore lifetime τ_seal ~ ms (small pores) to seconds (large pores). Membrane reseals if field duration is below the cumulative pore-widening threshold. Basis for clinical electrochemotherapy: bleomycin uptake increases 1000-fold at 50-80% DR. Ref: Mir et al. (1991), Weaver & Chizmadzhev (1996).
tip.drVibrating: Irreversible pore accumulation begins. Above V_thr, lipid reorganisation kinetics favour pore widening over resealing, the energy barrier for pore closure becomes positive. Lysis countdown starts: protocol requires N × t_p / dc seconds of sustained exposure. Reducing field amplitude here does not reliably prevent lysis.
tip.drLysing: Membrane integrity permanently lost, cytoplasmic release verified. For the simulation: lysis fires after lysisDelayMs = clamp(N × t_p / dc, 200 ms, 30 s). Cancer cells trigger first due to lower V_thr and larger R. Healthy cells at this DR indicate a protocol miscalibration, reassess amplitude or pulse parameters.
tip.tempHyper: Mild hyperthermia (41-45°C) has three independent therapeutic mechanisms: HSP upregulation that interferes with tumour immune evasion; mitotic spindle destabilisation preferentially in rapidly dividing cells; and membrane fluidisation that enhances drug and nanoparticle uptake by 2-10×. Synergistic with EP protocols. IAHT clinical window: 43°C × 60 min. Ref: Lepock (2003).
tip.tempDenat: Collagen triple-helix unravels at ~60°C; albumin denatures at ~68°C; cytoskeletal actin at ~75°C. These temperatures are achievable in tissue within seconds of high-amplitude CW-RF or HIFU exposure. Protein aggregation is largely irreversible, once denatured, enzymatic function and structural integrity are not recovered on physiological timescales.
tip.tempLysis: Water vaporisation drives membrane rupture via osmotic steam expansion. In pulsed nsPEF protocols peak temperatures can transiently exceed 100°C in the vicinity of the electrode surface while bulk medium stays cool. Relevant as an upper-bound check on pulse energy deposition, not a target operating point.
tip.tempCeil: Hard display ceiling in the simulation model, prevents visual overflow, not a physical limit. The Pennes bioheat / Newton-cooling model diverges above this point anyway (no phase-change term). In real tissue, ablative protocols operate at 50-90°C; values above 100°C represent instantaneous micro-zone temperatures, not bulk averages.
tip.tiPoor: DR_T / DR_H < 1.2× at the operating point. This can arise at f >> f_c(T) where Vm_T/Vm_H → (R_T × τ_H)/(R_H × τ_T), which can be below 1.0 for typical cancer/normal pairs. Also occurs when σ_i,T ≈ σ_i,H (no cytoplasmic contrast). In this regime pulse fractionation cannot rescue selectivity, the fundamental physics precludes a window.
tip.tiMarginal: 1.2-2.0× selectivity, field amplitude must be controlled to within ±5% to avoid healthy cell damage. In clinical IRE, electrode placement and impedance monitoring provide real-time feedback. Pulse fractionation (N pulses, spaced > τ_seal) allows selective accumulation of pore damage in faster-responding cancer cells without healthy cell recovery being outpaced.
tip.tiStrong: TI ≥ 2× indicates the cancer lysis field is ≤ 50% of the healthy lysis field. Gives a 2:1 amplitude safety margin. The adeno/hepatocyte pair achieves TI = 2.36× purely from size ratio + V_thr asymmetry at quasi-DC (TI = V_thr,H × R_T / (V_thr,T × R_H) = 1.1 × 15 / (0.70 × 10)), no frequency tuning required. This is the reference benchmark for evaluating other cell pairs.
tip.tiAblative: Healthy DR ≥ 85%, both cell types are in the irreversible EP zone. Not a failure mode per se: bulk ablation (prostate IRE, liver tumour ablation) intentionally operates here. The Ablative badge is a safety warning in the simulation context, signalling that selective targeting has been lost.
tip.winVmSel: Vm,DC = 1.5·E·R with cosθ = 1 (field-aligned pole). All other parameters, σ_e, σ_i, ε_r, d, frequency, cancel out at quasi-DC. This 1.5× is therefore the hard physical maximum imposed by the 15/10 µm size ratio; it cannot be improved by medium choice, waveform shaping, or frequency tuning. Only reducing R_H or increasing R_T (different cell pair) changes it.
tip.winTI: TI = E_lysis,H / E_lysis,T = (V_thr,H × R_T) / (V_thr,T × R_H) = (1.1 × 15) / (0.70 × 10) = 2.36×. Both terms contribute: size ratio alone gives 1.5×; the V_thr asymmetry multiplies this by 1.1/0.70 = 1.57×. Cancer membranes are structurally compromised (altered lipid composition, reduced cholesterol, elevated ceramide), lowering V_thr is a genuine biophysical difference, not a model artefact.
tip.winFreqDown: At f = f_c(T) ≈ 0.49 MHz, TI has already fallen to ~1.7× from 2.36×. At f >> f_c(H) ≈ 1.08 MHz: Vm_T/Vm_H → (R_T × τ_H)/(R_H × τ_T) = 0.68×, the cancer cell is actually HARDER to disrupt than the healthy cell because its longer τ_T means Vm rolls off sooner. This is the high-frequency selectivity reversal: operating above both f_c values is worse than not targeting at all.
tip.classVirus: R < 0.1 µm: Schwan quasi-DC Vm = 1.5·E·R ≤ 150 mV at 1000 V/cm, well below V_thr = 0.35-0.50 V. Pure EP is impractical. DEP crossover exists in the MHz range (relevant for dielectrophoretic capture). Acoustic resonance at ~10-12 GHz is inaccessible to RF hardware; f-laser experiments (Tsen et al.) used 100 mJ/cm² fluence, not V/cm.
tip.classBacteria: 0.1-2 µm: f_c ranges from ~5 MHz (R ≈ 1 µm, σ_e = 1.5 S/m) to several GHz (R ≈ 0.1 µm). The single-shell Schwan model is an approximation, gram-positive bacteria have a 20-80 nm peptidoglycan wall that should be modelled as an additional dielectric shell for accurate f_c prediction. Acoustic Q is viscoelastic (3-4), not crystalline.
tip.classMammal: R ≥ 2 µm: f_c in kHz-MHz range, accessible by standard function generators and RF amplifiers. Nucleus adds a second dielectric shell with distinct τ_ne. No rigid-shell acoustic resonance, mammalian cell membrane is a fluid lipid bilayer with no mechanical Q. The Schwan ωτ >> 1 roll-off at GHz frequencies is a dispersive loss, not a resonance.
tip.mediaSaline: σ_e = 1.5 S/m is the reference condition for all tabulated f_c and τ values. It maximises the contrast between σ_e and σ_i for mammalian cells, giving the largest τ sensitivity to intracellular parameter variation. The 0.9% NaCl solution is isotonic (~308 mOsm/kg), cell viability is maintained for 2-4 h in vitro.
tip.mediaBlood: σ_e ≈ 0.7 S/m varies ±15% with haematocrit (0.37-0.47). Lower σ_e extends τ and shifts f_c down. In intravascular tumour targeting (e.g., IRE via catheter), the blood σ_e sets the effective τ, f_c for a 15 µm cancer cell drops from 0.49 MHz (saline) to ~0.27 MHz (blood). This shifts the optimal frequency window accordingly.
tip.mediaTissue: σ_e ≈ 0.2 S/m models poorly-perfused tumour stroma. At this σ_e the Schwan τ formula gives τ ∝ 1/(2σ_e) as σ_e << σ_i, bulk Joule heating becomes a serious concern since P_medium ∝ σ_e·E². Lower σ_e buffers allow higher E with the same thermal budget.
tip.mediaWater: Distilled water σ_e ≈ 0.001 S/m, a theoretical extreme used as a boundary-condition reference. Practical electroporation in low-conductivity buffer uses σ_e = 0.01-0.1 S/m (sucrose or mannitol supplemented) to limit Joule heating while maintaining high E. At σ_e = 0.001 S/m, Ohmic dissipation per pulse is ~1000× lower than in saline.
tip.mediaPbs: PBS (Dulbecco's PBS, pH 7.4) σ_e ≈ 1.54 S/m. Composed of NaCl (137 mM) + KCl (2.7 mM) + Na2HPO4 (10 mM) + KH2PO4 (1.8 mM). Contains no nutrients, glucose, or bicarbonate. τ shift vs saline < 3%. Select PBS for short-duration EP assays (< 30 min) where medium-induced cell swelling is acceptable; use DMEM for viability assays requiring > 30 min recovery.
tip.mediaDmem: DMEM σ_e ≈ 1.50 S/m (Dulbecco 1959 formulation at 37°C). The τ shift vs saline is < 1%, negligible for Schwan model purposes. DMEM contains glucose (25 mM), sodium bicarbonate (44 mM), and L-glutamine (4 mM); these small-molecule solutes contribute minimally to σ_e at physiological concentrations.
tip.mediaRpmi: RPMI 1640 σ_e ≈ 1.55 S/m (Moore et al. 1967). Optimised for suspension growth of lymphocytes and haematological lines. Lower glucose (11.1 mM) and higher phosphate buffer than DMEM, osmolarity 290 mOsm/kg vs 320 mOsm/kg for DMEM. The τ difference vs saline is < 2%; select based on cell-line requirements, not Schwan model considerations.
tip.mediaMhb: Mueller-Hinton Broth σ_e ≈ 1.7 S/m. Slightly higher than saline, τ for mammalian cells decreases ~11%, raising f_c slightly. MHB is CLSI/EUCAST standard for MIC and bactericidal testing; using MHB as the electroporation medium enables direct comparison between EP lethality and antibiotic MIC on the same bacterial population.
tip.acousticSel: Theoretical upper bound assuming perfect Lorentzian coupling at f_res. In practice: RF hardware cannot reach 10-12 GHz at >1 kV/cm in a 1 mm electrode gap; near-field skin depth at GHz frequencies limits field penetration into the sample volume; and thermal noise at the cell scale (~k_B·T) competes with sub-thermal resonance amplitudes.
tip.acousticLorentz: L(f) = 1 / sqrt(1 + Q²·(f/f_res − f_res/f)²). At f_res: L = 1. FWHM = f_res/Q. For bacteria (Q ≈ 3-4): FWHM ≈ f_res/3.5. Practical implication: a 1% frequency offset at Q = 4 reduces coupling to L ≈ 0.98, tolerance is generous. For viral capsids (Q ≈ 28): a 1% offset gives L ≈ 0.45, frequency precision is critical.
